say.en: We have seen what a GPU is made of. Now we write programs for it. This video covers the parts of CUDA every program needs: launching a kernel, finding each thread's element, and moving data between the CPU and the GPU.
Here are the nine stages.
A whole program, kernels and the launch, choosing the number of blocks, and the grid-stride loop.
Then explicit memory and its cost, unified memory, checking for errors, and an exam question.
Stage 1: a complete program that adds two vectors of a million floats. First the kernel: the code one thread runs.
Each thread computes its global index, checks it is inside the array, and adds one pair of elements.
The host program allocates the arrays, launches the kernel with enough blocks of 256 threads to cover a million elements, and waits for the GPU.
Then it uses the result and frees the memory. Every CUDA program has this shape: prepare data, launch, wait, collect.
Stage 2: double-underscore global marks a kernel: it runs on the GPU and is called from the host.

do.text: Stage 2 of 9: kernels and the launch

say.en: Device functions run on the GPU and can be called only from GPU code. Host functions are ordinary CPU code, the default.
The triple angle brackets launch the kernel: blocks times threads copies of it, each with its own block and thread index.
The launch returns at once. The CPU carries on while the GPU works.
So before the CPU uses results, it must wait, with cudaDeviceSynchronize, or with a copy back, which waits by itself.
Stage 3: how many blocks? With n elements and T threads per block, we need the ceiling of n over T. In integer arithmetic, n plus T minus 1, divided by T.
A million elements, 256 per block: 3907 blocks.
That is 1,000,192 threads: 192 have no element.
That is why every kernel tests i less than n. Without the test, those 192 threads write past the end of the array.
And T: a multiple of 32, so no warp is half empty, and at most 1024. 128 to 512 is the usual choice.

do.text: blocks = (n + T − 1) / T, and test i < n

say.en: Stage 4: another style, the grid-stride loop. Each thread handles several elements, stepping by the number of threads in the whole grid.
The stride is block size times the number of blocks.
The loop starts at the thread's own index, and adds the stride until it passes n.
Now the grid can be any size. 80 blocks of 256 is 20,480 threads for a million elements.
Thread 0 handles elements 0, 20,480, 40,960, and so on: 49 of them. The last thread handles 48. Consecutive threads still touch consecutive elements, so every access stays coalesced.

do.text: grid-stride: any grid size, still coalesced

say.en: Stage 5: where do x and y live? The GPU has its own memory. In the explicit style there are two copies of each array: one on the host, from malloc, one on the device, from cudaMalloc.
cudaMemcpy with host-to-device copies the input over.
The kernel is given the device pointers. Passing a host pointer to a kernel is a common crash.
cudaMemcpy device-to-host brings the result back. It waits for the kernel first, so no separate synchronise is needed.
And both copies are freed: cudaFree on the device, free on the host.

do.text: malloc + cudaMalloc · copy in · launch · copy out

say.en: Stage 6: those copies are not free. Adding two arrays of a million floats moves 12 megabytes: two arrays in, one out.

do.text: Stage 6 of 9: what the copies cost

say.en: Over PCI Express at about 12 gigabytes per second, that is 1 millisecond.
The kernel itself reads and writes the same 12 megabytes from GPU memory at 224 gigabytes per second: about 0.054 milliseconds.
The copies take 19 times longer than the work. So keep data on the GPU across many kernels, and copy only at the start and the end.

do.text: copies can cost more than the kernel

say.en: Stage 7: unified memory. cudaMallocManaged returns one pointer that works on both the CPU and the GPU.
The CPU writes the array. When the kernel touches it, the pages migrate to the GPU on demand.
Synchronise before the CPU reads the result. Then the pages migrate back.
Each first touch is a page fault, which is slow. A prefetch call moves the data ahead of time.
Comparing them: explicit memory needs two pointers per array and copies written by you; unified memory needs one pointer and no copies.
Explicit gives you control, and is fastest when tuned. Unified is simpler, but pays for page faults unless prefetched.
Unified memory is good for learning, prototypes, and data with pointers inside it. Production code often moves data explicitly.
Stage 8: CUDA calls report errors through return values, and a kernel launch does not return one at all. This launch asks for 2048 threads per block, more than the limit of 1024.
Nothing crashes. The kernel simply never runs. cudaGetLastError right after the launch reports it.
Errors during the kernel's run, like reading outside an array, appear later, from the next synchronising call.

do.text: check after the launch and after the sync

say.en: Now an exam question: 10,000 floats, 256 threads per block.
Find the blocks and idle threads, one thread's element, the elements of two threads in a grid-stride loop of 8 blocks, and why a launch with 2048 threads does nothing. Pause and work it out.
a: 10,000 over 256, rounded up, is 40 blocks. 40 times 256 is 10,240, so 240 threads are idle.
b: block 17 times 256, plus 45: 4397.
c: 8 blocks of 256 gives a stride of 2048. Thread 100 handles 100, 2148, 4196, 6244 and 8292.
Thread 2000 handles 2000, 4048, 6096 and 8144; the next, 10,192, is past the end. 4 elements.
d: 2048 threads per block exceeds the limit of 1024, so the launch fails and z is never written. cudaGetLastError after the launch would say so.
The usual slip: forgetting the test i less than n, so the idle threads write past the end of the array.
Let us walk the stages again.
A kernel is launched with blocks and threads, returns at once, and needs the ceiling of n over T blocks, with a bounds test. A grid-stride loop works for any grid size.
Explicit memory copies data in and out, and those copies can cost more than the kernel. Unified memory is simpler. And launches must be checked for errors.
Next video: threads that cooperate. syncthreads, shared memory, and timing with CUDA events.
